solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Away result hurt

blocks.note: to be off is to be away, gone
an end is an outcome or result

explanation.surface: A football fan sums up the pain of losing an away match.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a sports report about a painful away defeat; really the first two words are joined end to end and the last word defines.
explanation.definitionFit: To offend someone is to wound their feelings, a direct verb synonym for causing hurt.

clue.text: A very fine meal is full of?

definitions.note: the question mark is a blank the answer fills to finish the sentence

indicators.note: something full of other things holds them inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: flour is finely ground meal
taken as written
V is the standard abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A diner praises a superb dinner and invites you to supply the missing word.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'A very fine meal is full of' as wordplay: FLOUR with A and V inside gives FLAVOUR, which also completes the sentence sensibly in place of the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is literally the missing word: a superb dinner is packed with taste, so the blank stands for the answer itself.

clue.text: Migrant guessed having cleared US borders

indicators.note: clearing something out removes it, so certain letters are taken away
a migrant moves from place to place, so the remaining letters wander into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; these two letters are removed

explanation.surface: An immigrant reckoned they had made it through American border control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US borders' looks like one phrase about frontiers, but US is the letters taken out of 'guessed' and 'borders' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Borders and edges are both the outer limits or margins of something, a plain plural noun synonym.

clue.text: Even with some sensible tips, Edward capsized

indicators.note: 'some' asks for only part of the following words, a run of consecutive letters
a capsized boat is upside down, and in a down clue that turns the letters to read upwards

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of sensible, all of tips and the start of Edward

explanation.surface: Edward's boat turned over even though he had been given good sailing advice.
explanation.walkthrough: The run E-TIPS-ED is read upwards to give DESPITE. 'Even with' opens the clue as if it were part of the story, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Despite means notwithstanding, so it swaps for 'even with' as a preposition introducing a contrary circumstance.

clue.text: Flat place at the rear aboard ship, quarter deck?

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept
being aboard a vessel means being inside it, so some letters go within others

blocks.note: a pad is informal slang for a flat or home
the final letter of place
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Someone looks for a level spot at the stern of a vessel, on its quarterdeck.
explanation.walkthrough: The quarterdeck is part of a ship, which fits the nautical surface; split into two words it becomes a card-playing idea, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Spades is one of four suits, so it makes up a quarter of a standard pack of playing cards.

clue.text: Senior priest continually spat behind piano

indicators.note: in a down clue what comes behind follows below, so the pieces are placed one after another

blocks.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
to go on is to continue without stopping
a spat and a tiff are both petty quarrels

explanation.surface: A senior cleric keeps spitting from behind the church piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spat' looks like the past tense of spit, but here it is a noun meaning a small quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Pontiff is a title for a high-ranking bishop, especially the Pope, so it names a senior priest.

clue.text: Five hundred and one words surprisingly get great results

indicators.note: something that turns out surprisingly is unexpected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500
taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A short 501-word piece of writing proves surprisingly effective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Five hundred and one' reads as one number, but it splits: the numeral for 500, then 'one' joins 'words' as the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To do wonders is an idiom for achieving remarkable success or producing excellent outcomes.

clue.text: Underwear Peter has but not Matthew?

blocks.note: Matthew is spelt with a doubled letter, so not like Matthew means not double: one only
the letter Peter contains just one of, while Matthew has two

explanation.surface: A question about what one apostle wears beneath his robes that another does not.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostles suggest Bible study, but the clue is about spelling: Peter contains SINGLE T, Matthew has two Ts. A singlet is a British vest worn under a shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless undershirt, a vest worn as an inner garment beneath outer clothing.

clue.text: Judge looks for this special case — but not yet

indicators.note: something special is out of the ordinary, so these letters are arranged in an unusual order

blocks.note: the four words taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A court judge examines an unusual case that has not yet come to trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' and 'case' pull toward the courtroom, but 'looks' is a noun: a pageant judge assesses appearance. 'Special' looks like part of 'special case' but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A pageant where judges rate entrants on their appearance is a competition, so judges there assess looks.

clue.text: Fruit Ann grows regularly collected by mother and child

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other letter is kept
things collected by someone are gathered inside their hold, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: ma is an informal word for mother
the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters
a teen is a young person, someone's child

explanation.surface: Ann's garden produce is gathered up by a mother and her youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grows' looks like a verb about gardening, but it only supplies letters; 'child' for a teenager is loose but fair, since a teen is still someone's offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: The mangosteen is a tropical fruit from Southeast Asia with a purple rind and sweet white flesh.

clue.text: Show you’re amused by secret tattoo on fellow’s back

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter
in an across clue, placing one thing on another puts it after, so they sit side by side

blocks.note: the final letter of fellow
ink is slang for a tattoo

explanation.surface: Someone smiles knowingly at a hidden tattoo on a man's back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secret tattoo' looks like a single phrase; 'secret' actually belongs to the definition, and 'fellow's back' gives only the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A wink is a conspiratorial closing of one eye, signalling shared knowledge or private amusement.

clue.text: Providing rules for a country walk

blocks.note: first meaning: relating to the founding law that governs a state
second meaning: a stroll taken for the sake of one's health

explanation.surface: Someone sets out regulations for a stroll through the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country walk' reads as one phrase about rambling; the split is after 'country', leaving 'walk' alone as the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a nation's founding law; as a noun it is an old-fashioned term for a healthy daily stroll.

clue.text: Magic year after heart’s broken by Romeo

indicators.note: a thing broken into has something forced inside it
one piece placed after another sits next to it in order

blocks.note: ticker is slang for the heart
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A year of enchantment follows Juliet's lover breaking someone's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo suggests Shakespeare's lover, but here it is simply the letter R from the phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Magic in the sense of conjuring illusions is deception, and trickery is the use of deceptive tricks.

clue.text: Fleshly pink around sweaty hole

indicators.note: going around something encloses it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: coral is a pinkish colour
sweat leaves the skin through pores

explanation.surface: A rather fleshy description of rosy skin around a perspiring opening.
explanation.walkthrough: The skin imagery of the surface carries through all three parts, so the definition hides in plain sight at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporeal means of the body rather than the spirit, matching the physical, bodily sense of fleshly.

clue.text: Bustling city centre safe for holiday

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letters
bustling means moving about busily, so the letters are jostled out of order

blocks.note: the two middle letters of city
taken as written

explanation.surface: A busy downtown is a secure spot to spend one's vacation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bustling city centre' reads as one place; 'bustling' is the signal to rearrange and 'city centre' gives only two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiesta is a festive celebration, originally a religious feast day in Spanish-speaking countries.

clue.text: Polish cereal lacking English instructions

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: to polish a surface is to rub it
rice is a cereal grain
E is the abbreviation for English; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A box of breakfast cereal from Poland comes without any directions in English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' at the start looks like the nationality; the capital is just the opening word, and it means to shine something.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubric is a set of directions heading an exam paper or liturgy, telling the reader what to do.

clue.text: Nudity PhD covered with university cape

indicators.note: something covered by another is wrapped in it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for university
a ness is a headland or cape, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness
a PhD holder is entitled to the title doctor, DR

explanation.surface: A doctoral graduate exposed apart from an academic cape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cape' looks like a cloak, fitting the graduation and nudity theme, but it is a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Undress as a noun means a state of having few or no clothes on, so it matches nakedness.

clue.text: Court holds up charge — case of illegal pictures on computer

indicators.note: a case surrounds its contents, so only the outer letters are kept
in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top
to hold something is to have it inside one's grasp

blocks.note: CT is the abbreviation for court
a rap is a criminal charge, as in 'take the rap'
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A court case about illegal images found on someone's computer is held up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holds up' reads as delaying the trial; it splits into the containment and the upward reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Clip art is ready-made graphics supplied with software for pasting into documents on a computer.

clue.text: Friend could be one of the enemy

definitions.text: Friend could be one of the enemy

blocks.clueFragment: Friend could be one of the enemy
blocks.note: surface reading: an ally might secretly be a traitor working for the other side
setter's reading: the word friend is the antonym of enemy

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a double agent; read as words, 'friend' is the antonym of 'enemy', and 'one of the enemy' also hints at someone on the other side.
explanation.definitionFit: Friend and enemy are antonyms, words of contrary meaning; also a contrary, the other side's player, is one.

clue.text: Police uncovered Ken Livingstone’s head in the Lords

indicators.note: removing the cover strips the outside letters, leaving the middle
the head of a word is its first letter
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: the middle letter once both ends are stripped
the first letter
the House of Lords is made up of peers

explanation.surface: Officers exposed Ken Livingstone, once London's mayor, as a member of the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Peelers is old British slang for police, after Sir Robert Peel who founded the Metropolitan Police; the two single letters go into the middle of PEERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Peelers is a historical nickname for British police constables, from the founder of the London force.

clue.text: Speak against bill that blocks peace agreement

indicators.note: something that blocks a passage sits inside it, plugging the gap

blocks.note: a truce is an agreement to stop fighting
an ad, or advert, is a bill posted up

explanation.surface: A politician argues against legislation that would obstruct a peace treaty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like parliamentary legislation; here it is a poster or advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: To traduce is to slander or malign someone, criticising them in damaging terms.

clue.text: Very little change in sea level

blocks.note: first meaning: an amount too small to matter
second meaning, read literally: a fall in the height of the sea

explanation.surface: Scientists report only a tiny shift in global sea levels.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is whimsical: a fall in the water's height is literally a drop in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a quantity so small relative to the need that it makes no real difference.

clue.text: Pinch someone occupying seat after The King and I

indicators.note: one piece placed after another follows it in sequence

blocks.note: CR stands for Carolus Rex, King Charles
taken as written
a Member of Parliament holds a seat in the Commons

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks into a theatre seat after a performance of the musical The King and I.
explanation.walkthrough: The King and I looks like the musical title; split up, it is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To crimp is to press or pleat something together, squeezing it as one would by nipping.

clue.text: Wallace designed trousers to give away

indicators.note: to trouser something is to pocket it, so the letters are held inside the neighbouring words

blocks.note: the last two letters of the first word and first two of the second

explanation.surface: Wallace makes a pair of trousers to hand out as a gift, as in Wallace and Gromit's The Wrong Trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like a noun for clothing, but it is a verb meaning pockets.
explanation.definitionFit: To cede territory or rights is to surrender them, handing them over to another party.

clue.text: Worried about Messi practising self-denial

indicators.note: being worried means being agitated, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Fans are anxious that the footballer Lionel Messi is on a strict diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worried about' reads as a phrase; 'about' belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An abstemious person restrains their appetite for food and drink, denying themselves indulgence.

clue.text: Salt in seawater, say, but missing initially in fish

indicators.note: missing at the start means the first letter is dropped
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: the word without its first letter
the sole is a flatfish

explanation.surface: A fish swims in salty seawater but seems to be missing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks salt as just one example of the definition. The fish surface fits the sea theme neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: A solute is a substance dissolved in a solvent, and salt dissolved in seawater is a classic example.

clue.text: Military engineer perhaps confused leaving hospital

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so a letter is taken out
confused means muddled, so the remaining letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hospital; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A disoriented army engineer is discharged from hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' looks like a hedge on the definition but supplies the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A sapper is a soldier of the Royal Engineers who builds fortifications, bridges and trenches.
